procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated April 17, 1969 of the Patna High Court in Govt. Appeal No. 28 of 1967 under sec. 417 ( 1) Cr. P.C.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Patna High Court heard Govt. Appeal No. 28 of 1967 and issued a judgment and order on April 17, 1969. The High Court held that the complaint was time barred.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State of Bihar appealed to the Supreme Court under Article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution of India, challenging the Patna High Court's judgment and order. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's decision.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Court at Dhanbad had the jurisdiction to entertain the complaint.

facts: Two primary questions were raised before the Supreme Court.
One question was about the jurisdiction of the court at Dhanbad to hear the complaint.
The second question was whether the complaint was filed too late and thus barred by the statute of limitations.
application: The Supreme Court acknowledged that both questions were fundamental to the case.
However, the Court decided to first address the question of whether the complaint was barred by limitation.
The Court explicitly stated that based on its view of the second question (limitation), it was not necessary to go into the first question (jurisdiction).
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court did not decide the issue of the Dhanbad court's jurisdiction. It resolved the case on the separate issue of the statute of limitations, finding that the complaint was filed too late. Because this finding was sufficient to dismiss the appeal, the Court declined to rule on the jurisdiction question.

issue.issue_text: Whether the complaint for failure to furnish annual returns was barred by limitation under s. 79 of the Mines Act 1952, or if the offence was a 'continuing offence' covered by the Explanation to the section.

facts: The respondents, owners of a stone quarry, failed to furnish their annual returns for the year 1959 by the prescribed deadline of January 21, 1960.
A complaint was filed against them for this failure on April 12, 1961, which was more than a year after the deadline.
law: Under Regulation 3 of the India Metalliferrous Mines Regulations, 1926, read with Section 66 of the Mines Act 1952, failing to furnish annual returns by January 21st of the succeeding year is a punishable offence.
Section 79 of the Mines Act 1952 states that a complaint for an offence must be made within six months from the date the offence was committed.
The Explanation to Section 79 provides an exception for a 'continuing offence', where the limitation period is computed with reference to every point of time during which the offence continues.
application: The Court analyzed the language of Regulation 3 to determine if the offence was a one-time event or a continuing one.
It found that the regulation makes the specific act of 'failure to furnish returns on or before January 21' the offence.
The Court reasoned that this infringement is complete on the day the deadline is missed. The offence occurs once and for all on that date.

The Court noted that neither Regulation 3 nor any other provision in the Act states that the continued non-compliance or continued operation of the mine without filing the returns constitutes an ongoing offence.
Therefore, the offence was not 'susceptible of continuance' and did not qualify as a 'continuing offence' under the Explanation to Section 79.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the failure to furnish annual returns was a one-time offence completed on January 21, 1960. Consequently, the offence fell under the main part of Section 79, which required a complaint to be filed within six months. Since the complaint was filed more than a year after the offence, it was barred by limitation (time-barred).

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Court at Dhanbad had the jurisdiction to entertain the complaint.
appellant_arguments: Inferred: The appellant (State of Bihar) implicitly argued that the Dhanbad court had jurisdiction to hear the complaint, as the complaint was filed there by the Chief Inspector of Mines, to whom the returns were due.
respondent_arguments: Inferred: The respondents, whose stone quarry was located in Bombay, argued that the court in Dhanbad lacked the territorial jurisdiction to entertain the complaint concerning their Bombay-based operations.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the complaint for failure to furnish annual returns was barred by limitation under s. 79 of the Mines Act 1952, or if the offence was a 'continuing offence' covered by the Explanation to the section.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the failure to furnish annual returns was a 'continuing offence' under the Explanation to Section 79 of the Mines Act. Therefore, the limitation period renewed every day the failure continued, and the complaint was not barred by time.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the offence was not a continuing one; it was completed on the specific date the deadline was missed (January 21, 1960). Therefore, the complaint was subject to the six-month limitation period under the main part of Section 79 and was filed too late.

cases.principle: Cited as an example of a continuing offence, where the failure to keep a factory in conformity with an Act (e.g., by leaving a flywheel unfenced) is an offence that continues every day the non-conformity persists.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An offense is committed once and for all when the prohibited act or omission occurs. For an offense to be considered a continuing offense, the relevant law must explicitly state that the continued disobedience or non-compliance is itself an offense; a failure to comply with a requirement by a prescribed date does not, on its own, constitute a continuing offense.
obiter: As in the case of a construction of a wall in violation of a rule or a bye-law of a local body, the offence would be complete once and for all as soon as such construction is made.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The failure to furnish an annual return by a specified deadline is an offence that is committed once and for all on the day the deadline is missed. It is not a 'continuing offence' because the act of omission is complete at that moment. A continuing offence requires an ingredient of continuance, such as a wrongful act that is repeated day after day, which is absent in the singular failure to file a document on time.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied a test to distinguish between a one-time offence and a continuing offence by determining if the offence contains an 'ingredient of continuance.' An offence committed 'once and for all' is complete upon the act or omission, whereas a continuing offence involves a wrongful act that persists or is repeated over time.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the appellant's argument that the failure to file was a continuing offence, finding instead that the infringement occurred on a specific date: January 21, 1960, when the owner failed to furnish the annual returns by that deadline.
The court reasoned that the default occurs on the last day allowed for filing the return, and at that point, the offence is complete. It is not an act that continues day after day.

The court distinguished this case from true continuing offences, such as failing to keep a factory in conformity with the Act (where the non-conformity exists every day) or using premises as a factory without a license (where the offence is committed every time the premises are used).
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the respondent's position that the offence was not a continuing one and was therefore subject to the standard limitation period under the main part of s. 79 of the Act.
The court's determination that the offence was completed on January 21, 1960, meant that the complaint filed on April 12, 1961, was lodged well outside the statutory limitation period.
Consequently, the court affirmed the High Court's holding that the complaint was time-barred.
